transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-20 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Markus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (AtlasHealth CTO), Liam O'Connor (Platform), Dr. Rosa Vega (ML Lead)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive on supporting 128k+ context for AtlasHealth long medical records use case; discussed chunking strategies, KV cache semantics, batching and latency tradeoffs, quantization, and VPC/on-prem options.
- Action items: Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet + recommended configs; Atlas to provide sample corpus and SLOs; schedule pilot planning.

Topics: long-context (128k+), chunking strategies, attention optimizations, KV cache/prefix caching, batching/throughput, quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem deployments, monitoring and rollout strategy.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Aisha: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros? we'll do a deep dive on the 128k long-context work and how Redwood can run this in dedicated or private setups.
[00:12] Priya: hi, Priya here. CTO. thanks. big focus is on ingesting entire multi-year patient histories, so the context lengths are... huge. 128K is the target.
[00:22] Markus: Markus from Redwood infra. I'll walk through runtime constraints, KV cache, and batching. there might be a few mis-heard words from auto transcription, sorry in advance.
[00:30] Liam: Liam, infra. we're particularly worried about latency tails and also KMS/HSM integration for PHI.
[00:36] Dr. Vega: Rosa, ML lead. we want to preserve retrieval-augmented generation fidelity across long docs. chunking strategy matters a lot.

[02:05] Markus: ok jumping in. high-level: supporting 128k+ requires combining attention optimizations (sparse/linearized attention variants or windowed attention), aggressive KV caching to avoid re-encoding the entire context on every request, and chunking at the application layer to keep per-infer seq lengths manageable.
[02:28] Priya: can you explain KV cache in practice? we've seen references to KV "cash" in some notes — is that the same?
[02:36] Markus: yes, kv cache — sometimes auto-transcript turns cache to cash — it's the token key/value cache that holds past keys/values per layer to avoid recomputation. for long context flows, we use two approaches:
[02:50] Markus: 1) Prefix KV caching: keep a frozen prefix in cache and only attend to deltas; 2) Chunked-attend: split the 128k into chunks (say 8–32k windows) and use a routing policy to fetch relevant chunks into working memory.
[03:12] Dr. Vega: for RAG scenarios, how do you keep retrieval context coherent across chunk boundaries? we don't want hallucinations because chunks are isolated.
[03:22] Markus: good point. we recommend overlap-based chunking plus cross-chunk summary tokens — so you store small dense summaries in the prefix cache and allow windows to rehydrate relevant summaries. that keeps coherence without blowing up per-step cost.

[05:10] Liam: what about attention optimizations? you mentioned sparse or linearized attention. how mature are those in Redwood runtime?
[05:22] Markus: we support a few execution paths. on the runtime we can select: full dense attention (baseline), block-sparse for long ranges, and a locality-window + global-exchange hybrid. the kernel selection happens at compile/runtime based on model architecture and sequence length distribution. for 128k we frequently route to a hybrid windowed attention with global tokens.
[05:47] Priya: and the latency? we're SLAing sub-2s for small queries but for long-doc reads we can accept higher but tail matters.
[05:55] Markus: right. if the request is a long-pass retrieval + short-generation, you can keep generate-time low by (a) preloading relevant chunks into the KV cache so generation only attends to a working set, and (b) using cached key/values to avoid O(L^2) compute for the whole 128k. typical numbers: warm-cached generation on a 32k working set hits p50 ~300ms, p95 ~1.2s on high-end GPUs; but cold loads that must read many chunks can push to multiple seconds. we'll share benchmark CSV with more concrete numbers.

[07:40] Priya: you mentioned preloading. does that mean we need an always-warm dedicated pool? or can hosted work with on-demand fetch?
[07:50] Aisha: good seller question. there are tradeoffs: hosted with intelligent routing and burstable dedicated nodes can work but if you need guaranteed warm KV for PHI-sensitive, heavy workloads, Dedicated or Private with pinned instances is safer. Dedicated gives predictable throughput; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you network control and KMS.
[08:12] Liam: we need KMS integration and audit logs — does Redwood Private support HSM?
[08:18] Markus: yes, Private supports customer KMS integrations and HSM via our on-prem package. we also provide per-request audit logs and token-level cost breakdowns in the Redwood Console.

[10:02] Dr. Vega: let's talk chunk sizing. what sizes do you recommend? 128k is big, but also a function of tokenization density.
[10:12] Markus: typical pattern: break the corpus into 8–16k token chunks with 512–2048 token overlap for context coherence. for some data (very verbose notes) you might choose 4–8k chunks. we also recommend building dynamic chunking in the retriever that can produce variable-sized chunks depending on semantic boundaries.
[10:39] Priya: overlapping increases cost though. any heuristics on overlap vs hallucination tradeoff?
[10:45] Markus: yes, overlap cost grows linearly with overlap size. empirically, 512–1024 tokens of overlap hits a good balance for medical notes where entity context spans paragraphs. we include an optional cross-chunk reranker and light summarization to reduce required overlap.

[13:05] Liam: how does batching work for these long-context requests? do we sacrifice latency for throughput?
[13:15] Markus: batching is the main lever for cost efficiency. continuous batching lets us aggregate many in-flight generations into single GPU kernels. with long-context you want small, latency-sensitive requests to bypass big-batch queues via priority routing. Redwood supports policy-based routing: latency-sensitive queries use a low-latency pool; high-throughput background jobs go to batch-optimized pools. you can also configure timeouts and batch sizes per route.
[14:02] Priya: what about memory — 128k causes huge KV memory. how do you manage per-tenant memory on shared infra?
[14:12] Markus: several strategies: (1) shard KV across GPUs and fetch only a working set; (2) use compressed KV formats (e.g., 8-bit keys/values) when acceptable; (3) eviction policies and warm checkpoints. for multi-tenant hosted we impose per-tenant cache quotas; for Dedicated/Private you can allocate larger caches.

[16:30] Aisha: question from sales side: cost delta for 8-bit quant vs full fp16 for long context. Markus?
[16:38] Markus: quantization reduces memory footprint substantially; 8-bit + int8 kernels can cut memory by ~2x–4x depending on format. performance depends on kernel support; in some cases int8 gives same throughput but slightly worse generation quality. for high-fidelity medical text we usually recommend Q4/8 configs in a canary to quantify quality impact. we'll share a comparison chart.

[19:12] Dr. Vega: any gotchas around QKKV caching with quantized weights? i.e., is the cache compatible or do we need double conversion?
[19:22] Markus: good question. the runtime keeps cache in a canonical internal format; we try to avoid conversions on the hot path. however, some older int8 kernels require layout transforms on load. Redwood's compiler will emit transform ops at load-time to minimize in-loop overhead. in practice you might pay a small cold-start penalty.

[21:00] Priya: we are curious about chunk summary techniques — you mentioned storing dense summaries in prefix cache. can you expand?
[21:12] Markus: sure — you produce a short embedding or compressed summary token per chunk. store those in a small prefix KV so when you route a request you first attend to summaries to pick which chunks to hydrate. this reduces working set size and helps retrieval precision. for compliance we keep summaries encrypted, and you can choose to keep them in your VPC-only store on Private.

[23:40] Liam: network egress and on-prem constraints: if we go Private or on-prem, can we still get Redwood Console telemetry?
[23:50] Aisha: yes we support private control plane options. telemetry can be proxied to Redwood console through a customer-controlled forwarder, or you can keep telemetry local with our console agent if needed. it depends on the compliance profile.

[25:55] Markus: showing a rough workflow: ingest -> chunk -> vectorize -> store embedding + summary -> retrieval -> select chunks -> preload KVs -> generation. for 128k the preload step is critical; you either keep a hot cache or pay for chunk fetch during request.
[26:20] Priya: can we pre-warm caches based on anticipated queries (e.g., clinical workflows)?
[26:25] Markus: yes, we support policy-driven prewarming (time-based, event-based), and you can add your own signals. prewarming requires reserved capacity for deterministic SLAs.

[28:10] Dr. Vega: how do you handle model rollouts for these heavy-kept caches? if we change model or quantization, cache invalidation is a pain.
[28:20] Markus: rollouts tie into the rollout subsystem: canary with cache-compatible variants, or full invalidation. we support compatibility metadata per model variant; if a new model has incompatible KV layout then we recommend staged rollout with warmers to rebuild caches gradually. there's also a fallback policy to a smaller model if warm cache isn't ready.

[31:02] Liam: we need deterministic auditing of which chunks were used per response for compliance. can you log that?
[31:12] Markus: yes, per-request trace includes chunk ids, retrieval scores, and model variant. in Private mode you can store those traces in your audit store; hosted mode we retain n days depending on plan.

[33:40] Priya: talk about benchmarks — what's in the CSV you mentioned?
[33:48] Aisha: it's a per-route set of numbers: cold vs warm p50/p95/p99, cost per request assuming certain batch sizes, memory footprint per shard, and suggested config (chunk size, overlap, quant). we'll attach it. link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/atlas-128k (placeholder link).

[36:00] Dr. Vega: for the retrieval component, does Redwood suggest a specific retriever? or is it agnostic?
[36:08] Markus: it's agnostic — we integrate with common vector stores and can run our own retriever. recommended flow is semantic retriever tuned to produce chunk-sized hits, with reranker for top-K. we can instrument the retriever pipeline.

[38:22] Priya: if we run on-prem GPUs, what hardware recommendations?
[38:30] Markus: for 128k with hybrid attention and reasonably large working sets, A100 80GB or equivalent L4/H100 clusters with NVLink are recommended. for cost-sensitive deployments, consider mixed pool: smaller GPUs for light-weight routes and large GPUs for heavy long-context jobs.

[41:00] Liam: what's the real-world throughput? like how many 128k reads/hour per 8xA100 cluster?
[41:10] Markus: depends on chunking and overlap. rough ballpark: if you prewarm key chunks and working set is ~32k, an 8xA100 cluster with sharded KV and optimized kernels might sustain hundreds of requests/hour with sub-second p50 for generation. without prewarm you can expect lower throughput. we'll provide a modeled estimate in the spreadsheet.

[44:05] Dr. Vega: are there model architecture constraints? e.g., some models don't support chunked attention easily.
[44:14] Markus: many modern encoder-decoder and decoder-only models can be adapted. however, model internals like rotary embeddings, ALiBi, or relative pos biases require runtime-aware kernel selection. when onboarding a model we run a verification suite to map compatibility and suggest quantization knobs.

[46:30] Priya: security checklist — SOC2, ISO, SSO?
[46:36] Aisha: Redwood has SOC2 Type II, ISO attestation options, SAML/SSO, RBAC, and per-route quotas. Private adds VPC peering or air-gapped deployment. we'll share compliance pack.

[48:55] Liam: any notes on billing — long context costs blow up per-token if naive. how do you present cost to product teams?
[49:04] Markus: Console breaks down token-level cost and attributes cost by chunk fetch + generation + storage. we also provide simulated cost models so you can run what-if scenarios when tuning overlap and batch size. plus Redwood Optimize recommendations can reduce per-token cost.

[51:20] Dr. Vega: latency-sensitive UI case: we want streaming for partial replies while retrieving. does streaming work with chunk hydration?
[51:30] Markus: yes — streaming works. typical approach: stream partial generation while background tasks hydrate more chunks; but ensure your UI handles mid-generation context updates. we expose streaming APIs and function-calling style outputs too.

[54:10] Priya: what about failure modes — if a chunk fetch fails mid-gen, what's fallback?
[54:18] Markus: default fallback is to gracefully degrade to available context and surface a warning; you can configure auto-fallback to a smaller model or canned reply. we also support retries and read-through caches.

[56:45] Aisha: quick commercial notes: Dedicated gives reserved capacity and warm caches; Private is better for strict compliance. Hosted can work but you must accept potential cold-starts unless you pay for reserved pools.

[59:10] Priya: thinking about pilot — we'd want Redwood to run a POC with our sample corpus and run both Hosted+Dedicates? Private?
[59:20] Aisha: typical pilot flow: (1) run hosted benchmark to validate models and configs; (2) move to Dedicated for warm-cache pilot + SLA; (3) if needed, plan Private on-prem pilot. each step collects metrics and quality evals.

[60:30] Markus: next, quick demo of the benchmark CSV — here are columns: model, variant, quant, chunk_size, overlap, warm_p50, warm_p95, cold_p50, cold_p95, mem_shard_gb, cost_per_req_usd.
[61:10] Priya: perfect. can you include an example config for a 32k working-set that includes exact runtime flags?
[61:20] Markus: yes we'll attach a sample runtime config snippet and a canary plan.
